title: HTML Forms and User Input
subtitle: Build accessible, reliable forms that collect information
description: Learn form structure, input types, labels, validation, selection controls, submission, and professional accessibility practices.

blocks.text:
## Page 1 — Understanding forms and how they work

Welcome back! Think about a website where a user creates an account, searches for a course, sends a message, or registers for an event. How does the website collect the information the user enters? One of the main HTML tools for this job is a **form**.

The `<form>` element groups controls that collect information from a user. These controls may include text fields, email fields, password fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdown lists, and buttons. The form provides a structure for collecting the values and, when configured, submitting them for processing.

A form does not automatically create a complete registration system or save information to a database. HTML describes the form and provides browser features such as basic validation. JavaScript can add client-side behavior, while a server or another suitable backend is normally responsible for securely processing submitted information, checking permissions, and saving data.

Two important form attributes are `action` and `method`. The `action` attribute identifies the URL or endpoint where the browser should submit the form. The `method` attribute describes how the browser sends the form data. `get` places form values in the URL query string and is useful for searches or requests intended to be shareable. `post` sends the form data in the request body and is commonly used when submitting information that should not be placed in the URL. POST does not, by itself, encrypt or secure the information; use HTTPS and appropriate server-side protections.

A form can contain labels, inputs, buttons, and other appropriate elements. Give each control a clear purpose, collect only the information you genuinely need, and explain what the user should enter. Professional forms are not simply collections of boxes: they help people understand what is required and complete the task correctly.

blocks.title: A simple contact form
blocks.code:
<form action="/contact" method="post">
  <label for="full-name">Full name</label>
  <input id="full-name" name="fullName" type="text" required>

  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Send message</button>
</form>
blocks.output: The form collects a name and email address. The labels identify the fields, required asks the browser to check that both fields have values, and submitting sends the form to the configured /contact endpoint. That endpoint must exist and handle the request for the submission to be processed.

blocks.question: A course website has a search form. The developer wants the search term to appear in the URL so a user can bookmark or share the search results. Which method is generally the best fit?
options: post, because all forms should hide their values in the request body
get, because search terms can be represented in the URL query string
put, because it is the standard HTML form method for searches
delete, because a search removes unrelated results
blocks.explanation: GET is suitable for searches whose results can be represented by a URL. This makes a search easier to bookmark or share. POST does not make data automatically secure, and standard HTML forms do not support PUT or DELETE as their direct method values in the same way as GET and POST.
blocks.hint: Consider which method naturally allows the search criteria to become part of a shareable URL.

blocks.text:
## Page 2 — Input types, names, and labels

The `<input>` element creates many different kinds of controls. Its `type` attribute tells the browser what kind of value the control is intended to collect. For example, `type="text"` is suitable for ordinary text, `type="email"` provides email-oriented input and basic browser validation, `type="password"` visually masks entered characters, `type="number"` is designed for numeric values, and `type="date"` can provide a date picker in supported browsers.

Other useful types include `tel` for telephone numbers, `url` for web addresses, `search` for search terms, and `checkbox` for an independent on/off choice. Choosing an appropriate type can improve mobile keyboard behavior and gives the browser more information about the data expected. A telephone number should not normally use `number`, because phone numbers may contain a plus sign, spaces, or leading zeros and are identifiers rather than quantities for arithmetic.

The `name` attribute is particularly important when a form is submitted. It supplies the field's key in the submitted data. The `id` attribute identifies an element in the page and can connect a `<label>` to its input. These attributes are not interchangeable: an input may have an id without a useful submission name, and a name alone does not automatically connect a visible label to the field.

A reliable label uses a `for` value that matches the input's `id`. For example, `<label for="email">Email address</label>` is associated with `<input id="email" name="email" type="email">`. Clicking the label can focus or activate the associated control, and assistive technology can announce the label when the field receives focus.

Placeholders are optional short hints shown inside an empty control, such as `name@example.com`. They are not a replacement for a label: the placeholder disappears as the user types, may have low contrast, and is not a dependable permanent description. Keep the label visible and use a placeholder only when an additional example or hint is useful.

blocks.title: Choosing appropriate input types
blocks.code:
<form action="/profile" method="post">
  <label for="phone">Phone number</label>
  <input id="phone" name="phone" type="tel" autocomplete="tel">

  <label for="birth-date">Date of birth</label>
  <input id="birth-date" name="birthDate" type="date">

  <label for="website">Website</label>
  <input id="website" name="website" type="url" placeholder="https://example.com">

  <button type="submit">Save profile</button>
</form>
blocks.output: The browser can offer a telephone-friendly keyboard, a date control, and URL-oriented input. The labels remain visible, and each input has a name for form submission. The placeholder is an example, not a substitute for the Website label.

blocks.question: A developer creates an input with id="student-email" and name="emailAddress", but writes <label for="email">Email address</label>. What is the main problem?
options: The input's name must always be identical to its id
The label's for value does not match the input's id, so the label is not properly associated with that input
Labels cannot be used with email inputs
The input must use type="text" for a label to work
blocks.explanation: A label's for attribute should match the id of the control it labels. Here, for="email" does not match id="student-email". The name is used for submitted data and does not have to match the id.
blocks.hint: Compare the value used by the label with the identifier on the input itself.

blocks.text:
## Page 3 — Required fields and browser validation

A good form helps users correct mistakes before the information is submitted. HTML provides several built-in validation attributes. The `required` attribute means a value must be supplied before the browser allows a normal form submission. It is useful for genuinely necessary fields, but do not mark every field required simply because you can. Collect only what the task needs.

For an email field, `type="email"` allows the browser to check whether the value has a basic email-like format. This is not proof that the address exists, belongs to the user, or can receive messages. Similarly, `type="url"` checks for a URL-like value; it does not guarantee that the website is safe or reachable.

The `minlength` and `maxlength` attributes set limits on text length. For numeric inputs, `min`, `max`, and `step` can constrain the values a browser accepts. For example, `type="number" min="1" max="10" step="1"` describes whole-number choices from 1 through 10. These constraints help the user, but the backend must still validate submitted data because requests can be made without using the page's normal interface.

Validation should be understandable. If a field is required, say so clearly. If a password has rules, explain those rules before submission rather than showing a vague error afterward. When errors occur, identify the field and explain how to correct it. Never rely on color alone to indicate an error; provide text or another clear cue as well.

Browser validation is useful, but it is not a security boundary. Users can change page code or send requests directly. A professional application repeats important checks on the server, handles unexpected input safely, and never trusts a value just because a browser accepted it.

blocks.title: A form with clear validation constraints
blocks.code:
<form action="/register" method="post">
  <label for="username">Username</label>
  <input
    id="username"
    name="username"
    type="text"
    minlength="3"
    maxlength="20"
    required
  >

  <label for="age">Age</label>
  <input id="age" name="age" type="number" min="13" max="120" required>

  <label for="account-email">Email address</label>
  <input id="account-email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>
blocks.output: The browser can check that the username is between 3 and 20 characters, the age is within the declared range, and the email has a basic email-like format. The server must still validate all submitted values before creating an account.

blocks.question: A registration form uses required and type="email". A user enters a syntactically plausible email address that does not actually exist. What can the browser's built-in validation establish on its own?
options: That the email account exists and belongs to the user
That the email address can definitely receive messages
That the field is non-empty and the value passes the browser's basic email-format check
That the registration is safe to save without any server-side checks
blocks.explanation: Required checks that a value was supplied, and type="email" checks a basic email-like format. Neither proves the mailbox exists or belongs to the user. Applications may need additional verification and must validate submitted data on the server.
blocks.hint: Separate checking the shape of a value from proving that the real-world value exists.

blocks.text:
## Page 4 — Checkboxes, radio buttons, select menus, and text areas

Not every question should use a plain text field. The control should match the kind of answer the user needs to provide. A checkbox is suitable for an independent choice that can be on or off, such as agreeing to receive optional updates. Multiple checkboxes can be selected when the user may choose several items.

Radio buttons are suitable when the user should select one option from a group, such as choosing one delivery method. To create a radio group, related radio inputs use the same `name` value and different `value` values. The name groups the choices for form submission, while each value identifies the chosen option. Give each radio input its own id and associated label so users can understand and select the choices.

A `<select>` element creates a dropdown list. Each available choice is usually represented by an `<option>` element. The option's value is the value submitted with the form; the text between its tags is what the user normally sees. If the value is omitted, the option text is generally used as its value, but explicitly writing meaningful values makes the form easier to maintain.

A `<textarea>` is used for longer, multi-line text such as a message, feedback, or a description. Unlike a single-line input, its initial text goes between the opening and closing tags. The `rows` attribute can suggest how many visible text lines it should show, while CSS can control its responsive width.

For related choices, use `<fieldset>` to group them and `<legend>` to give the group a title. For example, a legend such as “Preferred contact method” explains what a group of radio buttons is asking. This is especially useful when a form has several groups of choices, because each group needs context. Keep option wording clear and avoid forcing users to guess what a selection means.

blocks.title: A feedback form with grouped controls
blocks.code:
<form action="/feedback" method="post">
  <label for="message">Your feedback</label>
  <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="4" required></textarea>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>How should we contact you?</legend>

    <input id="contact-email" name="contactMethod" type="radio" value="email" required>
    <label for="contact-email">Email</label>

    <input id="contact-phone" name="contactMethod" type="radio" value="phone">
    <label for="contact-phone">Phone</label>
  </fieldset>

  <label for="topic">Feedback topic</label>
  <select id="topic" name="topic" required>
    <option value="">Choose a topic</option>
    <option value="course">Course content</option>
    <option value="technical">Technical problem</option>
    <option value="suggestion">Suggestion</option>
  </select>

  <button type="submit">Submit feedback</button>
</form>
blocks.output: The form collects a longer message, one contact preference, and a topic. The fieldset and legend describe the radio group. The empty-value prompt encourages the user to choose a real topic instead of accidentally submitting the prompt as a meaningful selection.

blocks.question: A survey asks the user to select exactly one preferred learning format: video, text, or audio. Which implementation best matches that requirement?
options: Three checkboxes with the same name, because checkboxes enforce one choice
Three radio inputs with the same name and distinct values, each with a clear label
Three text inputs, because users should type one of the formats
Three buttons without names or values, because button text is always submitted as form data
blocks.explanation: Radio inputs sharing a name form a single-choice group, and their distinct values identify the selected option. Checkboxes normally allow independent selections, while ordinary buttons do not automatically submit their visible text as a selected form value.
blocks.hint: Choose the control designed for one selection from a group of alternatives.

blocks.text:
## Page 5 — Submission, accessibility, security, and professional polish

A button inside a form commonly submits the form when its type is `submit`. A button with `type="button"` does not submit the form by default; it is useful for actions controlled by JavaScript, such as showing an extra section. A `type="reset"` button restores controls to their initial values, but reset buttons can surprise users and are often unnecessary in carefully designed forms.

Always give buttons an understandable label, such as “Send message” or “Save profile.” A vague label such as “Go” may not explain the result. Also make sure that a form can be used with a keyboard. Labels should be connected to controls, focus indicators should remain visible, and the page should not depend on a mouse or on color alone.

The `autocomplete` attribute can help the browser fill familiar information, such as a person's name, email, or telephone number. Use appropriate autocomplete tokens when they genuinely fit the field. This can make forms faster to complete, particularly on phones. Keep fields in a sensible order, use clear instructions, and avoid asking for information that is not needed.

Never treat HTML validation as protection for private information. Use HTTPS for data in transit, validate and sanitize inputs appropriately on the server, apply access controls, and protect sensitive operations. Password fields visually mask typing but do not encrypt a password. Do not put passwords, private messages, or other sensitive values into GET query strings, where they may appear in browser history, logs, or shared URLs.

Before publishing a form, test it on a narrow mobile screen and with a keyboard. Check that labels are readable, controls are easy to operate, required fields are clearly indicated, and error messages help people recover. Submit realistic test values and confirm the backend responds correctly. A professional form is complete only when its structure, usability, accessibility, and data-handling behavior work together.

blocks.question: A developer has built a form with required fields and browser validation. Before saving the submitted values to an account database, what is the most important additional responsibility for the server?
options: Trust the browser because required prevents users from bypassing validation
Repeat relevant validation and enforce security and permission rules on the submitted data
Remove all labels because the server receives field names instead
Convert every form method to GET so the submitted data can be inspected in the URL
blocks.explanation: Client-side validation can be bypassed by modifying the page or sending a request directly. The server must validate submitted data and enforce security and authorization rules before saving or acting on it. Labels improve the interface but do not replace server-side checks.
blocks.hint: Think about what happens when a request reaches the server without using the normal browser form.
